newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine sugar millers blame government for woes.
newsitem.headline: Philippine sugar millers blame government for woes.

text.p: Philippine sugar millers, pinched by an influx of cheap imports, pleaded on Sunday for government protection to enable the industry to compete with other sugar-producing countries.

"The Philippines has taken the industry for granted, never having granted subsidies, and even allowed the industry to slowly weaken," executives of 27 of the country's 36 sugar mills said in a joint letter to President Fidel Ramos.
Besides the 36 sugar mills, the Philippines also has 16 refineries. The millers said they had pumped more than five billion pesos into expanding their facilities in the past five years alone.
The Philippine sugar industry has been swamped in recent months by a flood of subsidised sugar from other countries which grant more protection to their sugar growers, the millers said.
"The playing field is sharply tilted against Philippine sugar," the letter said, a copy of which was released to the media.
The industry has asked the government to withdraw the 35 percent tariff discount on refined sugar imports from other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The tariff on sugar from non-ASEAN countries is scheduled to drop from 100 percent to 80 percent by July 1 as part of measures required before Manila can join the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
In five years, Manila will have only a 50 percent tariff on sugar imports, or half that in Indonesia and Thailand and a third of Mexico's under the tariff commitments to the WTO, the millers said.
"The United States, European Union and Japan will by then have tariffs nearly 300 percent higher than ours," the statement said.
The millers said it would then no longer be profitable for most sugar farmers to plant.
"As more farmers drop out, the sugar mills will suffer from capacity under- utilisation and lower efficiencies, pushing more mills into higher costs and eventual bankruptcy," they said.
The letter said the 35 percent tariff discount given to ASEAN sugar would result in losses for the local sugar industry amounting to over 40 billion pesos up to the next crop year (Sept/Aug).

Once a top Philippine export, sugar funded the lavish lifestyles of "sugar barons" in the 1970s under then-president Ferdinand Marcos. It also fuelled a communist rebellion as exploited farm workers rose up.
The privileges of the barons were curtailed when Corazon Aquino, after ousting Marcos in a 1986 popular revolt, launched a land redistribution programme that broke up large sugar plantations.
Of the 100,000 planters now cultivating the country's 370,000 hectares (925,000 acres) of sugar land, 80 to 90 percent own 10 hectares or less.
"Our industry asks no favour or subsidies but a clear and unequivocal policy to justify our continued investments, fortitude and very existence," the millers said.
"We need an environment no less than our competitors. We are willing to drop tariffs only if and when other countries do the same and at the rate no less favourable than theirs."
